problems.stem: A studio submission has eight beautifully polished frames, but a reviewer notes the sequence skips from defining photosynthesis straight to a quiz with no worked step between. What does this reveal about the storyboard?
options: Nothing; each frame is high quality, so the storyboard is strong.
The frames were optimized in isolation; the full sequence has a gap and does not carry the learner to the objective.
The quiz should simply be removed.
The frames need brighter colors.
problems.explanation: A studio submission is judged as a whole sequence. Excellent individual frames that leave a gap toward the objective still fail as a storyboard.

problems.stem: In one storyboard, Frame 2 gives the learner a Continue control to pace the content, but Frame 6 auto-advances through a dense multi-step procedure. What design flaw does this show?
options: Frame 6 should also be removed.
A principle (segmenting) was applied inconsistently across the storyboard, signaling an unintegrated design.
Continue controls are never appropriate.
The two frames should use the same color.
problems.explanation: Principles must hold across the whole storyboard. Honoring segmenting on one frame and breaking it on another shows the design was not integrated.

problems.stem: For the studio capstone, a learner pastes together the frame exercise, the image, the alt text, and the peer comments from earlier in the module with no connecting rationale. Why does this fall short of the studio's intent?
options: The artifacts should have been done in a different order.
The studio integrates the pieces into one defensible storyboard serving a single objective; a collection is not an integration.
Earlier artifacts may not be reused at all.
The capstone should contain only new work.
problems.explanation: The capstone asks the learner to integrate frame, modality, accessibility, and review decisions toward one objective, not to staple separate exercises together.

problems.stem: A learner submits a polished final storyboard for the studio with no other materials. Which addition would most raise the quality of the capstone as evidence of learning?
options: A higher-resolution export of the same storyboard.
A decision record listing the major design choices, the options rejected, and the principle or learner data behind each one.
A longer title slide.
More frames of the same kind.
problems.explanation: The capstone needs its evidence trail. A decision record of accepted and rejected choices, with warrants, is what turns a polished storyboard into defensible evidence of design judgment.

problems.stem: Your capstone objective is 'the learner can predict the next stage of the water cycle.' An AI tool suggests a sixth bonus frame on cloud types, and it is genuinely well designed. What is the defensible move?
options: Accept it; a well-designed frame always strengthens the sequence.
Accept it but place it last so it cannot interrupt the chain.
Reject it and record the reason in the decision record: it serves a second objective (cloud types), not the prediction objective, so it dilutes the sequence.
Reject it without documentation, since rejected suggestions do not belong in the package.
problems.explanation: The objective trace governs AI suggestions just like your own ideas: every frame must serve the single stated objective. A polished frame serving a different goal is exactly the seam that makes a capstone an assembly rather than an integration. The bounded AI move is to reject it and preserve the rejection, with its reason, in the decision record a reviewer can audit.
